PARALLAX

Beyond the frame.

Your camera records in two dimensions. How does editing software recover the third?

Imagine adding a glowing portal to a window in a video. As the camera moves around the building, the portal needs to stay on that window, turn with the wall, and appear smaller when the camera moves farther away. After Effects’ 3D Camera Tracker helps editors do this by estimating how the camera moved and where features in the scene sit in three dimensions. PARALLAX lets you place the portal, step outside the footage, and inspect the image measurements that hold it there. Pick a scene and add an effect of your own.

FIELD NOTES

How a flat video gives away the camera

Follow one window

A window corner leaves a distinctive patch of light and dark. Find that patch in the next frame and you have two pixel locations for the same place on the building.

Fit one camera move

A single camera movement must explain the tracks of many stationary corners at once. In an uploaded clip, the solver tries candidate movements, keeps the one supported by many tracks, then refines it to fit the pixels more closely.

Pin the text in space

Each pixel gives a line of sight. Seen from two camera positions, the lines converge near the window’s 3D location. Project a marker there through the moving camera and it stays attached to the window.

Why 2D and 3D tracking look different

A 2D track tells you where a corner appears on the screen. That’s enough to keep a label beside a window. A portal attached to the wall also needs to change shape with the viewing angle. A 3D track gives the portal a position in the scene, so the camera can project it from each new viewpoint.

Place a portal, pause the orbit with the wall at a slant, and switch tracking methods. Watch the rim: the 2D overlay keeps its original shape, while the 3D portal narrows into an oval as you see it from the side.

What this experiment knows about the camera

The observatory uses a fixed lens and a programmed camera path. The tracker works from the rendered images. Uploaded clips use an assumed focal length and estimated camera motion. Their depths are relative because the pixels cannot tell us how many meters the camera traveled. Moving subjects, zoom or too few distinctive corners can spoil a solve.

After Effects provides a full camera-tracking workflow. This lab isolates the geometry behind it. Adobe’s 3D Camera Tracker guide
